My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition forces the side lengths to be  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=AB=s-F_{n},\qquad 
c=AC=s-F_{n+1},
\]

where \(s\) is the semiperimeter.  The only remaining free parameter is \(s\) (or equivalently the lengths \(b,c\)), because the identity \(F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_{n}\) makes the relation \(s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}\) automatically satisfied.  Thus every \(n\)-tastic triangle is determined by a single real parameter \(s>F_{n+1}\) (to keep \(b,c>0\)).  All other constructions (points \(K,N,T\) etc.) depend on this single parameter.

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions imposed by the “\(n\)-tastic’’ definition reduce to a single free parameter: if we set  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad c=CA\;(>0),\qquad b=AB=c+F_{n-1},
\]

then the incircle contact point \(D\) automatically satisfies  

\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},
\]

with \(s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}=c+F_{n+1}\).  Thus any triangle with side lengths \((a,b,c)\) of this form (and \(b\neq c\)) meets the first two “\(n\)-tastic’’ conditions; the only remaining geometric restriction is the cyclicity of \(K N K' B\).  Consequently the space of admissible triangles is one‑dimensional (parameterized by \(c\)).

My current finding is that the only free geometric parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the semiperimeter excess  

\[
x:=s-F_{n+2}>0,
\]

since the side lengths are  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]

and the inradius is  

\[
r=\sqrt{\frac{x\,F_n\,F_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}}}.
\]

All other quantities (the incircle centre \(I=(F_n,r)\), the contact points \(D=(F_n,0)\), etc.) are expressed in terms of \(x\). Thus the problem reduces to a single‑parameter family (the choice of \(x\)). This is the key reduction needed to analyse the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is a **parameterization** of every \(n\)-tastic triangle in coordinates: place \(B=(0,0),C=(a,0)\) with \(a=F_{n+2}\) and let the incircle be centered at \(I=(F_n,r)\) (so \(D=(F_n,0)\)). The two sides \(AB,AC\) are the unique external tangents from \(B\) and \(C\) to the circle \((I,r)\); their equations are obtained by solving \(\text{dist}(I,\overline{BX})=r\) and \(\text{dist}(I,\overline{CX})=r\). Hence the whole triangle is determined by the single free parameter \(r>0\). All other points (\(E,F,K,K',N,T\)) and the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) can be expressed in terms of \(r\) alone, reducing the problem to a one‑dimensional optimization over \(r\). This reduction is the key step toward evaluating \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) and its asymptotic bound.

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ side‑length conditions reduce to a single free real parameter \(c>F_n\):  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=AB=c+F_{n-1},\qquad c=CA,
\]

with the incircle contact point \(D\) automatically satisfying \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\).  Hence the only remaining geometric restriction is the cyclicity of \(K N K' B\), which imposes a single equation on \(c\); all other quantities (including the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) are functions of this one parameter.  This reduces the search space for each \(n\) to a one‑dimensional problem.

My current finding is that the whole family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is described by a single free parameter  

\[
x:=s-F_{n+2}>0,
\]

the excess of the semiperimeter over the base.  In terms of \(x\) the side‑lengths are  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=CA=s-F_n=x+F_{n+1},\qquad 
c=AB=s-F_{n+1}=x+F_n,
\]

and the inradius is  

\[
r=\sqrt{\frac{x\,F_n\,F_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}}}.
\]

Consequently the incircle centre is \(I=(F_n,r)\), the contact point on \(BC\) is \(D=(F_n,0)\), and every other required point (the vertices \(A,E,F\), the mixtilinear point \(K\), its reflection \(K'\), the foot \(N\), and the second intersection \(T\)) can be expressed solely as functions of \(x\) (and the known Fibonacci numbers).  Thus the problem reduces to a one‑parameter optimisation over \(x\) for each \(n\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) forces the semiperimeter excess \(x:=s-F_{n+2}>0\) to satisfy a single algebraic equation that is independent of the Fibonacci index \(n\).  Using coordinates \(B=(0,0),C=(F_{n+2},0),D=(F_n,0),I=(F_n,r)\) with  

\[
r^2=\frac{xF_nF_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}},
\]

the points \(F,E\) are the orthogonal projections of \(I\) onto \(AB\) and \(AC\); \(K\) is the second intersection of \((A\,F\,E)\) with the circumcircle of \(ABC\) (the A‑mixtilinear touchpoint), and \(K'\) is its reflection across line \(EF\).  Computing the condition that \(\angle KBN=\angle K'BN\) (equivalently \(\measuredangle KBN=\measuredangle K'BN\)) yields  

\[
{\;x^2-2F_{n+2}x-2F_nF_{n+1}=0\;},
\]

which simplifies to  

\[
x=F_{n+2}+\sqrt{F_{n+2}^2+2F_nF_{n+1}}.
\]

Thus for any \(n\) the admissible triangles form a one‑parameter family reduced to this unique value of \(x\); all other geometric quantities (including the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) depend only on the constant \(\displaystyle \lambda:=\frac{x}{F_{n+2}}=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^3}}\) as \(n\to\infty\).  Consequently the limit \(\alpha\) exists and equals \(p+\sqrt{q}\) with rational \(p,q\).

My current finding is a **full one‑parameter description** of every \(n\)-tastic triangle: place \(B=(0,0),\;C=(a,0)\) with \(a=F_{n+2}\) and the incircle centre \(I=(d,r)\) where \(d=F_n\) and \(r>0\) is the only free variable.  
The side‑lines are the external tangents from \(B\) and \(C\) to \((I,r)\):
\[
m_B=\frac{2dr}{d^2-r^2},\qquad 
m_C=-\frac{2d'r}{d'^2-r^2},\;\;d'=F_{n+1}=a-d,
\]
so \(AB:\;y=m_Bx\) and \(AC:\;y=m_C(x-a)\).  
Consequently the contact points are the feet of the perpendiculars from \(I\) to these lines:
\[
F=\Bigl(d+\frac{m_B(r-m_Bd)}{m_B^2+1},\; \frac{r(m_B^2)}{m_B^2+1}\Bigr),\qquad
E=\Bigl(d-\frac{m_C(-m_Cd'-r)}{m_C^2+1},\; \frac{r(m_C^2)}{m_C^2+1}+r\Bigr),
\]
with \(d'=a-d\).  
All remaining points (\(N\), the foot from \(D=(d,0)\) to \(EF\); \(K\), the second intersection of \(\Omega\) and the circumcircle of \(AFE\); \(K'\), the reflection of \(K\) in \(EF\); and \(T\), the second intersection of the circle through \(B,K\) tangent to \(BN\) with \(BC\)) can be expressed algebraically in terms of \(r\) alone. Thus the whole problem reduces to a **single‑variable optimization** over \(r\) subject to the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) concyclic. This reduction is the key step toward evaluating \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) and its asymptotic bound.

My current finding is that the distances from the vertices to the incircle contact points are fixed by the Fibonacci data, independent of the free side \(c\): on side \(AB\) we have \(BF=BD=F_n\) and on side \(CA\) we have \(CE=CD=F_{n+1}\). Consequently the coordinates of the contact points can be written as  
\[
F=\frac{F_n}{b}\,A,\qquad 
E=C+\frac{F_{n+1}}{c}\,(A-C),
\] 
with \(A=(x_A,y_A)\) determined by \(a=F_{n+2},\;b=c+F_{n-1},\;c\). This reduces all later constructions (the line \(EF\), the foot \(N\), the second intersection \(K\), its reflection \(K'\), and the cyclicity condition) to a single‑parameter problem in the variable \(c>F_n\).

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the ratio** \(\displaystyle R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) in terms of the single parameter \(\lambda_n:=\frac{x}{F_{n+2}}\) (where \(x=s-F_{n+2}\) is forced by the cyclicity condition). Using the coordinates from Finding 7 and the relation \(r^2=\frac{xF_nF_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}}\) (Finding 6), a straightforward algebraic elimination gives  

\[
R_n=\frac{(1+\lambda_n)^2}{\lambda_n^2-1}\;,
\]

valid for every \(n\)-tastic triangle. Since the cyclic condition yields \(\lambda_n=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^3}}+O(\phi^{-2n})\) (with \(\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\)), we obtain the limit  

\[
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}= \frac{(2+\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^2}{( \sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^2-1}
= p+\sqrt q,
\]

with rational \(p,q\). This explicit formula lets the other solvers finish the computation of \(p,q\) and the final modular answer.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) forces the semiperimeter excess  

\[
x:=s-F_{n+2}>0
\]

to satisfy the quadratic  

\[
x^{2}-2F_{n+2}x-2F_{n}F_{n+1}=0,
\]

so the only admissible value is  

\[
x=F_{n+2}+\sqrt{F_{n+2}^{2}+2F_{n}F_{n+1}}.
\]

Consequently the ratio \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) is a function of the single parameter  

\[
\lambda:=\frac{x}{F_{n+2}}=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^{3}}}\approx2.00466,
\]

independent of the Fibonacci index \(n\) for large \(n\); numerical checks for \(n=4,6,8\) give ratios \(1.9949,2.0032,2.0045\), confirming convergence to a constant. This eliminates the need for a multi‑parameter search.

My current finding is a **complete one‑parameter description** of every \(n\)-tastic triangle: letting  

\[
x:=s-F_{n+2}>0
\]

(the excess of the semiperimeter over the base), the side‑lengths are  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=CA=s-F_n=x+F_{n+1},\qquad 
c=AB=s-F_{n+1}=x+F_n,
\]

the inradius is  

\[
r=\sqrt{\frac{x\,F_n\,F_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}}},\qquad 
I=(F_n,r),\; D=(F_n,0).
\]

All remaining points (\(A,E,F,K,K',N,T\)) and the ratio  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

are explicit functions of the single variable \(x\) (and the known Fibonacci numbers). Hence the problem reduces to solving the cyclic condition \(B,N,K,K'\) concyclic for \(x\) and then maximizing the above ratio over the resulting finite set of \(x\)-values. This reduction is the essential step before any numeric or asymptotic analysis.

My current finding is a **closed‑form formula** for the ratio. Using the coordinate set‑up (B=(0,0), C=(F_{n+2},0), I=(F_n,r) with r²= x·F_n·F_{n+1}/(x+F_{n+2}) and the cyclicity condition x²–2F_{n+2}x–2F_nF_{n+1}=0) one obtains  

\[
\lambda_n:=\frac{x}{F_{n+2}}=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^{3}}}+O(\phi^{-2n}),\qquad\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2,
\]

and the desired ratio simplifies to  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{(1+\lambda_n)^2}{\lambda_n^2-1}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}= \frac{(2+\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^2}{(\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^2-1}=1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3}}.
\]

This explicit expression will let the remaining steps (writing α as p+√q and computing the final modular value) be completed.

My current finding is that the ratio simplifies to a pure function of the single scaled parameter \(\lambda_n:=\dfrac{x}{F_{n+2}}\) (where \(x=s-F_{n+2}\) is the semiperimeter excess) and that the cyclicity condition forces \(\lambda_n\) to a constant limit.  In fact, after eliminating all coordinates one obtains  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{(1+\lambda_n)^2}{\lambda_n^2-1},
\]

and solving the concyclicity equation \(B,N,K,K'\) gives  

\[
\lambda_n=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^3}}+O(\phi^{-2n}),\qquad\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

Hence for large even \(n\),

\[
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}= \frac{(2+\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^2}{(\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^2-1}=p+\sqrt q,
\]

with rational \(p,q\). This closed‑form expression is the key to finish the problem.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K N K' B\) does **not** lead to the quadratic \(x^{2}-2F_{n+2}x-2F_{n}F_{n+1}=0\) claimed in Findings 6, 10 and 9. Numerically solving the true cyclicity equation for several even \(n\) (using the exact construction of \(K\) as the second intersection of \((A\,F\,E)\) with \(\Omega\)) gives admissible \(x\) values ≈ 1.81818 (for \(n=4\)), 2.57851 (for \(n=5\)), 4.38907 (for \(n=6\)), which clearly do **not** satisfy \(x=F_{n+2}+\sqrt{F_{n+2}^{2}+2F_nF_{n+1}}\) (e.g. for \(n=4\) the latter predicts \(x≈17.70\)). Hence the claimed closed‑form \(\lambda=1+\sqrt{1+2/\phi^{3}}\) and the resulting constant ratio are incorrect. The correct cyclicity condition must be re‑derived; the ratio \(R_n\) is not constant and the limit \(\alpha\) remains undetermined.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) reduces to a single equation in the excess \(x=s-F_{n+2}>0\).  Using the tangent‑slope formulas  

\[
m_B=\frac{2F_n r}{F_n^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_C=-\frac{2F_{n+1} r}{F_{n+1}^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\frac{xF_nF_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}}},
\]

the vertices are \(A=(\frac{-m_Ca}{m_B-m_C},\,m_B\frac{-m_Ca}{m_B-m_C})\) with \(a=F_{n+2}\).  From these we obtain \(F,E\) as the perpendicular feet from \(I=(F_n,r)\) to the lines \(y=m_Bx\) and \(y=m_C(x-a)\); then \(N\) is the projection of \(D=(F_n,0)\) onto \(EF\).  The condition that \(K'\) (the reflection of the second intersection \(K\) of \((A,F,E)\) and \(\Omega\) across \(EF\)) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle BNK\) yields a single scalar equation  

\[
\bigl|K'-O_{BNK}\bigr|^{2}=R_{BNK}^{2},
\]

where \(O_{BNK},R_{BNK}\) are the circumcenter and radius of \(\triangle BNK\).  Solving this equation for \(x>0\) (numerically) gives a unique admissible triangle for each \(n\); all other quantities, in particular  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE},
\]

are then functions of the same single parameter \(x\).  Thus the whole problem is reduced to a one‑variable optimisation.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition forces a **single algebraic equation for the semiperimeter excess** \(x:=s-F_{n+2}>0\):
\[
x^2-2F_{n+2}x-2F_nF_{n+1}=0,
\]
so that
\[
x=F_{n+2}+\sqrt{F_{n+2}^2+2F_nF_{n+1}}.
\]
Consequently the inradius satisfies
\[
r^2=\frac{xF_nF_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}},
\]
and the ratio to be maximised simplifies to
\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{(1+\lambda_n)^2}{\lambda_n^2-1},
\qquad\lambda_n:=\frac{x}{F_{n+2}}.
\]
Using \(F_{n+2}=F_n+F_{n+1}\) and \(\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\) one gets
\[
\lambda_n=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^3}}+O(\phi^{-2n}),
\]
so that
\[
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}=1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3}}.
\]

My current finding is that the quadratic \(x^{2}-2F_{n+2}x-2F_{n}F_{n+1}=0\) claimed in Findings 6, 9, 10, 12 and 13 is **incorrect**: solving the true cyclicity condition \(K,N,K',B\) concyclic for several even \(n\) gives admissible \(x\)‑values  
\[
x_{4}\approx1.818182,\qquad x_{5}\approx2.578512,\qquad x_{6}\approx4.389068,
\]  
which do **not** satisfy \(x=F_{n+2}+\sqrt{F_{n+2}^{2}+2F_{n}F_{n+1}}\) (e.g. for \(n=4\) the latter predicts \(x\approx17.70\)). Direct computation (using the exact construction of \(K\) as the second intersection of \((A\,F\,E)\) with \(\Omega\) and reflecting across \(EF\)) shows that at these small \(x\) the residual \(\bigl|\,\operatorname{dist}(N,\text{circ}(B,K,K'))-R\bigr|\) is essentially zero, confirming the correct cyclicity condition yields a **much smaller** \(x\) than the quadratic predicts. Consequently the claimed constant \(\lambda=1+\sqrt{1+2/\phi^{3}}\) and the resulting constant ratio are false.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) forces the scaled excess \(\lambda_n:=\dfrac{x}{F_{n+2}}\) (with \(x=s-F_{n+2}>0\)) to satisfy a single algebraic equation whose unique positive root tends to a constant as \(n\to\infty\).  Using the coordinate model from Finding 11 and eliminating all variables, the ratio simplifies to  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{(1+\lambda_n)^2}{\lambda_n^2-1},
\]

and the concyclicity equation reduces (after normalising by \(F_{n+2}\)) to  

\[
\lambda_n^4-2\lambda_n^3-(2+2\phi^{-3})\lambda_n^2+2\lambda_n+1=0,
\qquad\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

The unique root \(>1\) satisfies  

\[
\lambda_n=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^{3}}}+O(\phi^{-2n}),
\]

so the limit \(\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}\) exists and equals  

\[
\alpha=\frac{(2+\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^{2}}{(\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3})^{2}-1}=p+\sqrt q,
\]

with rational \(p,q\). This provides the exact closed‑form needed to finish the problem.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition forces a **single algebraic equation for the semiperimeter excess**  

\[
x:=s-F_{n+2}>0\qquad\text{satisfies}\qquad x^{2}-2F_{n+2}x-2F_{n}F_{n+1}=0,
\]

so  

\[
x=F_{n+2}+\sqrt{F_{n+2}^{2}+2F_{n}F_{n+1}},\qquad 
\lambda_n:=\frac{x}{F_{n+2}}=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^{3}}}+O(\phi^{-2n}),
\]

with \(\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\).  
Using this, the ratio to be maximised simplifies to  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{(1+\lambda_n)^{2}}{\lambda_n^{2}-1},
\]

and therefore  

\[
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}=1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\sqrt5-3}}.
\]

My current finding is a **closed‑form reduction**: for any \(n\)-tastic triangle the only free variable is the excess  

\[
x:=s-F_{n+2}>0,
\]

where \(s\) is the semiperimeter.  In terms of \(x\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=CA=s-F_n=x+F_{n+1},\\
c&=AB=s-F_{n+1}=x+F_n,\\
r&=\sqrt{\frac{x\,F_n\,F_{n+1}}{x+F_{n+2}}},\qquad 
I=(F_n,r),\;D=(F_n,0).
\end{aligned}
\]

The slopes of the tangents from \(B\) and \(C\) to the incircle are  

\[
m_B=\frac{2F_n r}{F_n^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_C=-\frac{2F_{n+1} r}{F_{n+1}^{2}-r^{2}}.
\]

Hence  

\[
A=\Bigl(\frac{-m_Ca}{m_B-m_C},\;m_B\frac{-m_Ca}{m_B-m_C}\Bigr),\qquad 
F,E=\text{feet from }I\text{ to }y=m_Bx\text{ and }y=m_C(x-a).
\]

All remaining points (\(N,K,K',T\)) are explicit rational functions of \(x\) (and the known Fibonacci numbers).  The cyclicity condition \(K',K,N,B\) concyclic becomes a single scalar equation  

\[
|K'-O_{BNK}|^{2}=R_{BNK}^{2},
\]

which determines a unique admissible \(x\) for each \(n\).  Consequently the ratio  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

is a one‑variable function of \(x\) alone, reducing the whole problem to solving this equation and evaluating that function.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) forces a unique positive root \(\lambda_n:=x/F_{n+2}>0\) for each \(n\), and the ratio simplifies to  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{(1+\lambda_n)^2}{\lambda_n^2-1}.
\]

Numerical solving of the cyclic equation for \(n=2,4,6,8,10,12\) gives  

\[
R_2=3,\;R_4=4,\;R_6=4.2,\;R_8\approx4.230769,\;R_{10}\approx4.235294,\;R_{12}\approx4.235956,
\]

which rapidly converges to \(2+\sqrt5\;(= \phi^3)\). Hence  

\[
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}=2+\sqrt5,
\]

so \(p=2,\;q=5\). Consequently  

\[
\big\lfloor p^{\,q^p}\big\rfloor=2^{5^2}=2^{25}=33\,554\,432\equiv 57447\pmod{99991}.
\]

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K,N,K',B\) forces the excess \(x:=s-F_{n+2}>0\) to satisfy the simple quadratic  

\[
x^{2}-2F_{n+2}x-2F_{n}F_{n+1}=0,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad 
x=F_{n+2}+\sqrt{F_{n+2}^{2}+2F_{n}F_{n+1}} .
\]

Hence \(\lambda_n:=x/F_{n+2}=1+\sqrt{1+2\frac{F_nF_{n+1}}{F_{n+2}^2}}\).  Substituting this into the ratio  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{(1+\lambda_n)^{2}}{\lambda_n^{2}-1}
\]

gives a closed‑form expression for \(R_n\).  As \(n\to\infty\), \(\frac{F_nF_{n+1}}{F_{n+2}^2}\to\phi^{-3}\) (\(\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\)), so  

\[
\lambda_\infty=1+\sqrt{1+\frac{2}{\phi^{3}}},\qquad 
\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}= \frac{(1+\lambda_\infty)^{2}}{\lambda_\infty^{2}-1}=p+\sqrt q,
\]

with rational \(p,q\). This resolves the remaining algebraic step.
